beats.say: A man faces north. He turns 135 degrees to the left, then 225 degrees to the right. Which way does he face at the end?

ask.ifNot: Compare the two numbers. 225 is more than 135, so the right turn is the bigger one.

beats.say: Here is the key idea. A left turn and a right turn are opposites, so they undo each other. Which of his two turns is bigger?
So the left turn cancels part of the right turn. What is left over is 225 take away 135.
Taking away 125 would leave 100, and 10 more away leaves 90. So all his turning comes to just 90 degrees to the right.

ask.ifNot: Picture a compass, with north at the top. A quarter turn to the right goes the way clock hands move, and that takes you to east.

beats.say: 90 degrees is a quarter turn. Start facing north and make a quarter turn to the right. Where do you face?
East. He ends up facing east.
The trap is to stop after the first turn. 135 to the left only takes him to south-west, and he still has the big right turn to make.
So with left and right turns, cancel first. Take the smaller from the bigger, then make the turn that is left.
Our angle is 35 degrees. It has two partners, its complement and its supplement. We find both, then add them together.

ask.ifNot: A square corner is a right angle, a quarter turn. That is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: First the complement. Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. How much do they make together?
So the complement is 90 take away 35. 90 take away 30 is 60, and 5 more away leaves 55.

ask.ifNot: The two angles on the line make 180 together. So take 35 away from 180.

beats.say: Now the supplement. Supplementary angles sit together on a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees. Which sum gives the supplement?
180 take away 35. Here is a quick way: 180 is 90 more than 90, so the supplement is 90 more than the complement. 55 and 90 make 145.
Careful now. The question wants the sum of the two partners. Not the angle itself. Just the complement and the supplement.
55 plus 145. The tens first: 50 and 140 make 190. Then the ones: 5 and 5 make 10. Altogether, 200.
So the sum is 200 degrees.
Two partners, two take aways, one addition. Complement from 90, supplement from 180, then add.
An angle is one fifth of its supplement. We have to find the angle.

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: First, what do an angle and its supplement make together?
Now think in equal parts. If the angle is 1 part, its supplement is 5 of those parts, because the angle is one fifth of it. Here is the picture.

ask.ifNot: Count both bars. 1 part for the angle and 5 parts for the supplement. Together that is 6 parts. The trap is to count only the 5.

beats.say: How many equal parts make the whole 180 degrees?
1 and 5 make 6 parts. Those 6 equal parts share 180 degrees.
So one part is 180 divided by 6. 6 times 30 is 180, so one part is 30.
The angle is 1 part. So the angle is 30 degrees.
Let's check. The supplement is 180 take away 30, which is 150. And one fifth of 150 is 30. It works.
So when one angle is a fraction of the other, count all the parts, share out the total, and check.

board.text: Supplement of an obtuse angle is always ...?

beats.say: Take any obtuse angle and find its supplement. The question says the supplement is always the same kind of angle. Which kind?

ask.ifNot: Obtuse means wide open. It is bigger than a right angle, 90 degrees, but smaller than a straight line, 180 degrees.

beats.say: First, how big is an obtuse angle?
Let's try one. 110 degrees is obtuse. Its supplement is what is left of the straight line: 180 take away 110, which is 70.

ask.ifNot: Small, sharp angles, less than 90 degrees, are called acute.

beats.say: 70 is less than 90. What do we call an angle that is smaller than a right angle?
Acute. But does it always happen? Try a very wide one, 170 degrees. 180 take away 170 leaves only 10. Acute again.
Here is why. The straight line is 180, which is two lots of 90. The obtuse angle takes more than 90 of it. So what is left must be less than 90.
So the supplement of an obtuse angle is always an acute angle.
On a straight line, the two partners balance. If one is wider than a square corner, the other must be narrower.
Start with 48 degrees. We need its complementary angle and its supplementary angle, and then the sum of those two.

ask.ifNot: A square corner is a right angle, a quarter turn. That is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: First the complement. Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. How much do they make together?
So the complement is 90 take away 48. 90 take away 40 is 50, and 8 more away leaves 42.

ask.ifNot: The two angles on the line make 180 together. So take 48 away from 180.

beats.say: Now the supplement. Supplementary angles sit together on a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees. Which sum gives the supplement?
180 take away 48. Here is a quick way: 180 is 90 more than 90, so the supplement is 90 more than the complement. 42 and 90 make 132.
Careful now. The question wants the sum of the two partners. Not the angle itself. Just the complement and the supplement.
42 plus 132. The tens first: 40 and 130 make 170. Then the ones: 2 and 2 make 4. Altogether, 174.
So the sum is 174 degrees.
So the plan is: take the angle from 90, take the angle from 180, and add the two answers.
Here is 48 degrees. The question wants two other angles, the complement and the supplement, added together.

ask.ifNot: A square corner is a right angle, a quarter turn. That is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: First the complement. Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. How much do they make together?
So the complement is 90 take away 48. 90 take away 40 is 50, and 8 more away leaves 42.

ask.ifNot: The two angles on the line make 180 together. So take 48 away from 180.

beats.say: Now the supplement. Supplementary angles sit together on a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees. Which sum gives the supplement?
180 take away 48. Here is a quick way: 180 is 90 more than 90, so the supplement is 90 more than the complement. 42 and 90 make 132.
Careful now. The question wants the sum of the two partners. Not the angle itself. Just the complement and the supplement.
42 plus 132. The tens first: 40 and 130 make 170. Then the ones: 2 and 2 make 4. Altogether, 174.
So the sum is 174 degrees.
Remember the two totals. 90 for complementary, 180 for supplementary. Find each partner, then add.
What is the angle between the two hands of a clock at 20 past 7? Here is the clock.
A clock has 12 numbers, so the full turn of 360 degrees is cut into 12 equal gaps. Each gap is 360 divided by 12, which is 30 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps: 4 to 5, 5 to 6, 6 to 7. That is 3 gaps.

beats.say: At 20 minutes past, the minute hand points at the 4. Count the gaps from the 4 to the 7.
3 gaps of 30 make 90 degrees. That takes us from the 4 up to the 7.

ask.ifNot: 20 minutes is one third of an hour. So the hour hand has gone one third of the way from the 7 to the 8.

beats.say: Here is the trap. At 7:20 the hour hand is not on the 7 any more. It has been creeping towards the 8 for 20 minutes. How far has it gone?
One third of a gap is 30 divided by 3, which is 10 degrees.
So the angle is the 90, plus the extra 10. That makes 100 degrees.
So count the gaps, 30 degrees each, then add the bit the hour hand has crept on. It never waits on its number.

board.text: South-west, turns clockwise to north. Degrees = ?

beats.say: A man is walking south-west. He turns clockwise until he faces north. How many degrees does he turn?
A compass has 8 directions, and they share a full turn of 360 degrees. So each step to the next direction is 360 divided by 8, which is 45 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Clockwise from south-west we pass west, then north-west, then we reach north. That is 3 steps. 5 steps is the other way round.

beats.say: Now go clockwise from south-west, the way clock hands move. How many steps is it to north?
West, north-west, north. 3 steps.
3 steps of 45. 2 of them make 90, and 45 more makes 135.

choices: No, so it is None of these
ask.ifNot: Read the choices again. 90, 225 and 180 are there, but 135 is not. When our answer is not listed, we pick None of these.

beats.say: So he turned 135 degrees. Now look at the choices. Is 135 there?

board.text: 135° is not listed: None of these

beats.say: 135 is not on the list. So the answer is None of these.
225 is the trap. It is the turn the other way round, anticlockwise. Trust your working, even when the answer is None of these.

board.text: Angle between the hands at 18 minutes past 5 = ?

beats.say: What is the angle between the hands at 18 minutes past 5? The hands do not land neatly on the numbers, so we measure how far each hand has turned from the top of the clock.
The minute hand goes all the way round, 360 degrees, in 60 minutes. So each minute it turns 360 divided by 60, which is 6 degrees.
In 18 minutes it turns 18 times 6. 10 sixes are 60 and 8 sixes are 48, so that is 108 degrees.

ask.ifNot: From the 12 to the 5 is 5 gaps, and each gap is 30 degrees. 5 times 30 is 150.

beats.say: Now the hour hand. From one number to the next is 30 degrees. At 5 o'clock exactly, how far round from the 12 is it?
5 times 30 is 150. But here is the trap. In 18 minutes the hour hand has crept on, past the 5.
The hour hand takes 60 minutes to cross one gap of 30 degrees. So it moves 1 degree every 2 minutes. In 18 minutes, that is 9 degrees.
So the hour hand is at 150 and 9 more, which is 159 degrees.
The angle between the hands is the gap between those two. 159 take away 108 leaves 51.
So the angle is 51 degrees.
Measure both hands from the 12, then subtract. And don't forget the hour hand's little creep: 1 degree for every 2 minutes.

board.text: Which pair of angles is supplementary?

beats.say: We have 4 pairs of angles, and only one pair is supplementary. We have to test them.

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What must a supplementary pair add up to?
So we add each pair and look for exactly 180. First pair: 62 and 128. The 2 and the 8 make 10, and 60 and 120 make 180. That is 190. Too much.
Second pair: 73 and a half, and 107 and a half. The whole numbers, 73 and 107, make 180. Then the two halves make 1 more. 181. So close!
Third pair: 85 and a half, and 93 and a half. 85 and 93 make 178, and the two halves make 1 more. 179. Just short.

ask.ifNot: Two halves make 1 whole. So we add 1 more to 179, and that makes 180.

beats.say: Last pair: 140 and a half, and 39 and a half. The whole numbers, 140 and 39, make 179. What happens when we add the two halves?
179, and 1 more from the two halves. Exactly 180.
So the supplementary pair is 140 and a half degrees, and 39 and a half degrees.
Did you see how close the others were? 181 and 179. Near enough is not good enough. Supplementary means exactly 180.

board.text: A line segment has how many end points?

beats.say: How many end points does a line segment have? Let's picture one.
Think of a piece of string pulled tight between your two hands. That is a line segment: a straight path with a start and a stop.

ask.ifNot: Put one finger on A, where it starts, and another on B, where it stops. That is 2 end points.

beats.say: I have named the two ends A and B. Count the points where the segment stops.

board.text: A line segment has 2 end points

beats.say: 2 end points. One at each end.
Now compare. A ray starts at a point and goes on for ever one way, like the beam of a torch. It has only 1 end point.
And a line goes on for ever both ways. It has no end points at all.
So a line has no ends, a ray has 1, and a line segment has 2. Only the segment has a length you can measure.

board.text: How many lines pass through two distinct points?

beats.say: Mark two different points, A and B. How many straight lines can pass through both of them?

ask.ifNot: Put your ruler on the point and keep turning it, like the spokes of a wheel. Every turn gives a new line. There is no limit.

beats.say: Start with just one point, A. How many lines can pass through a single point?

board.text: Through 1 point: lines in every direction

beats.say: Through one point, lines can go in every direction, like the spokes of a wheel.

choices: No, it is held in place
ask.ifNot: Try it with a ruler and two dots. Once the ruler touches both dots, any turn makes it slip off one of them.

beats.say: Now the line must pass through B as well. Lay your ruler so it touches A and B together. Can you still turn it?
The two points pin the ruler down. Only one straight line fits through both.
So through two distinct points, exactly one line can pass.
That is why we can name a line by just two of its points, like line A B. Two points, one line.

board.text: Three or more points on the same line are called?

beats.say: What do we call three or more points that all lie on the same line?
Here are three points, A, B and C, all sitting on one straight line, like beads on a string.

board.text: co + linear = together + on a line

beats.say: The word we want has two pieces. Co means together, as in co-operate. And linear comes from the word line.

ask.ifNot: Listen for the word line hiding inside it. Co, together, and linear, on a line: collinear. Parallel and concurrent are words about lines, not about points.

beats.say: So what do we call points that lie together on one line?
Collinear. Points on the same line are collinear points.

board.text: Not all on one line: non-collinear

beats.say: If one point steps off the line, the three are no longer all on one line. Then we call them non-collinear.
A quick test: lay a ruler along the points. If one straight edge touches them all, they are collinear.

board.text: An angle less than 90° is called?

beats.say: Angles get their names from how wide they open. Our measuring stick is the right angle, the square corner of a page. That is 90 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture. As the two arms close up, the angle gets narrow and pointed, like the tip of a pencil.

beats.say: Now close the angle up a little, so it is less than 90. Does it look sharper or blunter than the square corner?
Sharp and pointed. The word for that is acute. Acute means sharp.

board.text: It is called an Acute angle

beats.say: So an angle less than 90 degrees is called an acute angle.
Here are the other names, so you can tell them apart. Exactly 90 is a right angle. More than 90 but less than 180 is obtuse. Exactly 180 is a straight angle.
A way to remember: a cute little angle. Acute angles are the small ones.
A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of your book. How many degrees is it?
Start with a full turn. Spin all the way round until you face the same way again. That is 360 degrees.

ask.ifNot: A quarter means one of 4 equal parts. So we share 360 into 4 equal parts. That is 360 divided by 4.

beats.say: A right angle is a quarter turn. 4 square corners fit round a point, like the place where 4 floor tiles meet. So how do we find one quarter of 360?
360 divided by 4. Half of 360 is 180, and half of 180 is 90.
So a right angle measures 90 degrees.
Check: 4 right angles make 4 times 90, which is 360. One full turn.
So a quarter turn is 90, a half turn is 180, and a full turn is 360. Keep those three in your pocket.

board.text: An angle of 180° is called a?

beats.say: What do we call an angle of 180 degrees? Let's see what it looks like first.

ask.ifNot: 180 and 180 make 360. So 180 is half of a full turn.

beats.say: A full turn is 360 degrees. What part of a full turn is 180?
Two lots of 180 make 360. So 180 degrees is a half turn.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture. One arm goes left and one goes right. Together they lie flat, in one straight line.

beats.say: Point one arm ahead of you. Now turn the other arm half way round. The two arms point in opposite directions. What shape do they make?
A straight line. So an angle of 180 degrees is called a straight angle.
The other names in the list: a right angle is 90, a reflex angle is bigger than 180, and a complete angle is the full 360.
The name tells you the picture. Straight angle, straight line, 180 degrees.
What type of angle is 135 degrees? Here it is.
To name an angle, we compare it with two fence posts: 90 degrees, the right angle, and 180 degrees, the straight line.

ask.ifNot: 135 has a hundred in it, and 90 does not reach a hundred. So 135 is the bigger number.

beats.say: First fence post. Is 135 more than 90, or less?
More than 90. So it is wider than a square corner. It cannot be acute, and it cannot be a right angle.
Second fence post. 135 is less than 180, so it has not opened as far as a straight line. It cannot be reflex.

ask.ifNot: Acute is for angles under 90. Reflex is for angles over 180. The band in between, from 90 to 180, is called obtuse.

beats.say: So 135 sits between 90 and 180. What is the name for an angle in that band?
Obtuse. 135 degrees is an obtuse angle.
So to name any angle, ask two questions. Is it past 90? Is it past 180?

board.text: Two angles that add up to 90° are called?

beats.say: Two angles add up to 90 degrees. So together they fill a square corner, like this. What is such a pair called?
Here is an example: 30 degrees and 60 degrees. Together they make 90, a perfect square corner.

ask.ifNot: Say them aloud. Complete, complementary. They start the same way. Supplementary is for two angles that make a straight line.

beats.say: Each angle completes the other to make the corner. One of the names sounds like the word complete. Which one?
Complementary. Two angles that add up to 90 degrees are complementary angles.
Its cousin is supplementary: two angles that add up to 180 degrees, a straight line.
Here is how to keep them apart. C for complementary, C for corner. S for supplementary, S for straight.
And the other two names say where angles are, not what they add up to. Adjacent means next door. Vertically opposite means across a crossing.
Three angles lie side by side on a straight line. Two of them are 48 degrees and 67 degrees. We want the third.

ask.ifNot: Angles side by side on a straight line make a half turn together. A half turn is 180 degrees. 360 is for angles all the way round a point.

beats.say: What do the angles on a straight line add up to?
So all three angles together make 180. First, add the two we know.
48 and 67. 40 and 60 make 100. 8 and 7 make 15. So that is 115.

ask.ifNot: 115 is the two angles we were given, added together. The third angle is the piece that is still missing from the straight line.

beats.say: We have 115. Is that our answer?
The third angle is what is left of the 180. Take away 100 first, which leaves 80. Then 15 more, which leaves 65.
So the third angle is 65 degrees.
Check by adding all three: 115 and 65 make 180. One whole straight line.
So for angles on a line: add what you know, then take it away from 180.

board.text: 8 equal slices, 3 eaten. Angle of the rest = ?

beats.say: A pizza is cut from the centre into 8 equal slices, and Ria eats 3. What angle do the remaining slices make at the centre?

ask.ifNot: All the way round a point is a full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees. 180 is only half way round.

beats.say: All the slices meet at the centre, and together they go the whole way round. How many degrees is the whole way round?
360 shared among 8 equal slices. Half of 360 is 180, half of 180 is 90, and half of 90 is 45. So each slice is 45 degrees.

ask.ifNot: There were 8 slices to begin with, and 3 are eaten. 8 take away 3 leaves 5.

beats.say: Ria eats 3 of the 8 slices. How many slices are left?
5 slices are left, and each one is 45 degrees.
5 times 45. 4 slices are half the pizza, which is 180 degrees. One more slice of 45 makes 225.
So the remaining slices make an angle of 225 degrees.
A check: the 3 eaten slices make 135. And 135 and 225 make 360, the whole pizza.
135 is the trap. It is the part that was eaten. Always look at which slices the question asks about.

board.text: Hour hand, 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. Degrees turned = ?

beats.say: How many degrees does the hour hand turn between 3 p.m. and half past 7 the same evening?
The hour hand goes once round the clock, 360 degrees, in 12 hours. So in 1 hour it turns 360 divided by 12, which is 30 degrees.

ask.ifNot: From 3 to 7 is 4 hours. Then there is half an hour more, up to half past 7.

beats.say: How long is it from 3 p.m. to half past 7?

board.text: 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. = 4 and a half hours

beats.say: 4 whole hours, and then half an hour.
For the 4 whole hours, the hand turns 4 times 30, which is 120 degrees.
Don't stop there! The hour hand keeps moving during the last half hour. Half an hour gives half of 30, which is 15.
120 and 15 make 135. The hour hand turns through 135 degrees.
The hour hand is slow but steady. 30 degrees for every hour, and 15 for every half hour.

board.text: Facing East. Three-quarter turn anticlockwise. Now?

beats.say: Arjun faces east. He makes a three-quarter turn anticlockwise. Which way does he face now?
A quarter turn takes you from one main direction to the next. A three-quarter turn is 3 of those, one after another.

ask.ifNot: Clock hands go from east down to south. Anticlockwise is the other way, so from east we go up to north.

beats.say: Anticlockwise means the opposite way to clock hands. Starting from east, which direction comes first going anticlockwise?
First quarter turn: east to north.
Second quarter turn, still anticlockwise: north to west.
Third quarter turn: west to south.
So Arjun is facing south.
A neat check: three quarters anticlockwise lands in the same place as one quarter clockwise. And one step clockwise from east is south.
Take quarter turns one at a time, and always check which way round you are going.

board.text: Ladder makes 58° with the ground. With the wall = ?

beats.say: A ladder leans on a wall and makes 58 degrees with the ground. What angle does it make with the wall? Look: the ladder, the wall and the ground make a triangle.

ask.ifNot: Upright meeting level makes a square corner, like the corner of a room. A square corner is a right angle, 90 degrees.

beats.say: The wall stands upright and the ground is level. So what angle do the wall and the ground make?
The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees. The right angle uses 90 of that. So the other two angles share what is left: 90.

ask.ifNot: The two ladder angles make 90 together, and one is 58. So take 58 away from 90. Taking it from 180 forgets the right angle.

beats.say: So the two angles at the ends of the ladder make 90 together. One of them is 58. Which sum finds the other?
90 take away 50 is 40, and 8 more away is 32.
So the ladder makes an angle of 32 degrees with the wall.
Check: 58 and 32 make 90, and the right angle adds 90 more. 180 in all.
In a triangle with a right angle, the other two angles always make 90 together.

board.text: 6:00: angle is 180°. How much smaller at 6:30?

beats.say: At 6 o'clock the hands make a straight line, 180 degrees. By 6:30 the angle is smaller. We want to know how much smaller.

ask.ifNot: The hour hand moves too. In half an hour it goes half of the way from the 6 to the 7.

beats.say: First we need the angle at half past 6. The minute hand has gone half way round, and now it points at the 6. Where is the hour hand?
Halfway between the 6 and the 7. That is the first trap. If it had stayed on the 6, the two hands would be together.
One gap between two numbers is 30 degrees, because 360 shared among 12 gaps is 30. So half a gap is 15.
So at half past 6, the angle between the hands is just 15 degrees.

choices: No, how much smaller it became
ask.ifNot: The question says: by how many degrees has the angle become smaller. So we compare 180 at the start with 15 now.

beats.say: Now read the question again. Does it ask for the angle at 6:30?
The angle went from 180 down to 15. The drop is 180 take away 15, which is 165.
So the angle has become smaller by 165 degrees.
Two traps in one question. The hour hand creeps, and the question asks for the change, not the new angle. Read the last line twice.

board.text: Full turn every 40 seconds. Turn in 15 seconds = ?

beats.say: A lighthouse lamp makes one full turn every 40 seconds, at a steady speed. How many degrees does it turn in 15 seconds?

ask.ifNot: A full turn takes you all the way round, back to where you started. That is 360 degrees.

beats.say: How many degrees is one full turn?
So the lamp turns 360 degrees in 40 seconds.
Find the turn in 1 second first. 360 shared among 40 seconds. Cross a zero off each number: 36 divided by 4, which is 9.

ask.ifNot: Each second gives 9 degrees, and there are 15 seconds. So it is 15 times 9.

beats.say: 9 degrees every second. Now, which sum gives the turn in 15 seconds?
15 times 9. 10 nines are 90, and 5 nines are 45. 90 and 45 make 135.
So the lamp turns through 135 degrees.
Does that make sense? 15 seconds is less than half of 40 seconds. And 135 is less than half a turn, 180. Good.
Find what happens in 1 second, then multiply. That works for anything that turns at a steady speed.
The supplement of an angle is 3 times its complement. We must find the angle. There is a lovely idea hiding in here.

ask.ifNot: Both start from the same angle. One goes up to 90 and the other goes up to 180, which is 90 further. So the supplement is always 90 more.

board.text: Complement: tops the angle up to 90°
Supplement: tops the angle up to 180°

beats.say: Take any angle. Its complement tops it up to 90. Its supplement tops it up to 180. So how much bigger is the supplement than the complement?
180 is 90 more than 90. So the supplement is always the complement, plus 90.
Now use the clue. The supplement is 3 times the complement. Picture the complement as 1 block. Then the supplement is 3 of those blocks.

ask.ifNot: 2 equal blocks make 90, so each block is half of 90. That is 45.

beats.say: The supplement has 2 blocks more than the complement. And we know the extra is 90. So 2 blocks make 90. How big is 1 block?
Half of 90 is 45. So the complement is 45 degrees.
The angle and its complement make 90. So the angle is 90 take away 45, which is 45 as well.
Check. The supplement of 45 is 180 take away 45, which is 135. And 3 times 45 is 135. It works.
The key was one fact: a supplement is always 90 more than the complement of the same angle.

board.text: Lines cross: one angle = 4 × the one beside it. Largest?

beats.say: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 4 times the angle beside it. We want the largest angle.

ask.ifNot: Angles side by side on a straight line make a half turn together. A half turn is 180 degrees. 360 is for all 4 angles round the point.

beats.say: Two angles beside each other at a crossing sit on one straight line. So what do those two add up to?
Now think in parts. Call the smaller angle 1 part. The angle beside it is 4 times as big, so it is 4 parts.

ask.ifNot: 1 part for the small angle and 4 parts for the big one. 1 and 4 make 5 parts.

beats.say: How many parts make the 180?
5 parts make 180, so one part is 180 divided by 5. 5 thirties are 150 and 5 sixes are 30. So 5 times 36 is 180. One part is 36.
36 is the small angle. The big one is 4 parts, 4 times 36. Double 36 is 72, and double 72 is 144.
Opposite angles at a crossing are equal. So the 4 angles are 144, 36, 144 and 36. The largest is 144 degrees.
Check: 36 and 144 make 180, a straight line.
36 is the trap. It is the small angle, and the question wants the largest. And angles beside each other share a straight line, so they share 180, not 360.

board.text: Round a point: 80° and 4 equal angles. Each = ?

beats.say: 5 angles meet at a point and fill the whole turn. One is 80 degrees, and the other 4 are equal. How big is each equal angle?

ask.ifNot: All the way round a point is a full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees. 180 is only half way round.

beats.say: The angles fill the whole turn round the point. How many degrees is that?
First take away the angle we know. 360 take away 60 is 300, and 20 more away is 280.

ask.ifNot: There are 5 angles in all, but the 80 has already been taken out. Only the 4 equal angles share the 280.

beats.say: 280 is left for the equal angles. How many angles share it?
280 shared among 4. 28 divided by 4 is 7, so 280 divided by 4 is 70.
So each of the equal angles is 70 degrees.
Check: 4 times 70 is 280, and 80 more makes 360. A whole turn.
Take away what you know, then share the rest. And share it only among the angles that are still unknown.

board.text: Smaller angle between the hands at 2:40 = ?

beats.say: What is the smaller angle between the hands of a clock at 2:40? Here is the clock.
The 12 numbers cut the full turn of 360 degrees into 12 equal gaps. Each gap is 30 degrees.
At 40 minutes past, the minute hand is on the 8. Measure from the top of the clock, the 12. From the 12 round to the 8 is 8 gaps, and 8 times 30 is 240.

ask.ifNot: 1 degree for every 2 minutes. 40 minutes is 20 lots of 2 minutes. So the hour hand moves 20 degrees.

beats.say: Now the hour hand. At 2 o'clock it is 2 gaps from the top, 60 degrees. But it moves 30 degrees in 60 minutes: 1 degree every 2 minutes. How far does it move in 40 minutes?
20 degrees. So the hour hand is at 60 and 20 more: 80 degrees from the top.
The angle between the hands is the difference. 240 take away 80 is 160.

The trap is to leave the hour hand on the 2. From the 2 to the 8 is 6 gaps, which would be 180. But the hour hand has crept 20 degrees closer.
So the smaller angle is 160 degrees.
Measure both hands from the top of the clock, then subtract. And remember that the hour hand never sits still.

board.text: 2:10 to 2:50. Minute hand turn − hour hand turn = ?

ask.ifNot: Both times are in the same hour. From 10 minutes past to 50 minutes past is 50 take away 10, which is 40 minutes.

beats.say: First, how much time passes from 2:10 to 2:50?
40 minutes pass.
The minute hand does a full turn, 360 degrees, in 60 minutes. That is 6 degrees every minute. So in 40 minutes it turns 40 times 6, which is 240.

ask.ifNot: 1 degree for every 2 minutes. 40 minutes is 20 lots of 2 minutes, so the hour hand turns 20 degrees.

beats.say: The hour hand is much slower. It crosses one gap of 30 degrees in 60 minutes. That is 1 degree every 2 minutes. So how far does it turn in 40 minutes?
20 degrees. A small turn, but it counts.

ask.ifNot: How many more asks how far ahead the minute hand is. That is a difference, so we take the smaller turn away from the bigger one.

beats.say: The question says how many more. Do we add the two turns, or subtract?
240 take away 20 is 220. The minute hand turns 220 degrees more.
240 is the minute hand alone and 20 is the hour hand alone. Both are waiting in the choices. Only the difference answers how many more.

board.text: From 12 noon the hour hand turns 75°. Time = ?

beats.say: At 12 noon the hour hand points straight up. Later it has turned exactly 75 degrees. What time is it?

ask.ifNot: 360 degrees shared among 12 hours is 30 degrees for each hour.

beats.say: The hour hand goes right round, 360 degrees, in 12 hours. So how far does it turn in 1 hour?
30 degrees every hour.
So every 30 degrees is 1 hour. How many 30s fit into 75? 30 and 30 make 60. One more 30 would be 90, which is too many. So 2 whole hours.
2 hours use up 60 degrees. 75 take away 60 leaves 15 degrees still to explain.

ask.ifNot: 30 degrees takes a whole hour. 15 is half of 30, so it takes half an hour, and half an hour is 30 minutes. The degrees are not the minutes.

beats.say: 15 degrees is half of 30. So how much time does that last bit take?
Half of the turn, so half of the hour: 30 minutes.
So 2 hours and 30 minutes have passed since 12 noon. The time is 2:30 in the afternoon.
The trap is to read degrees as if they were minutes. The hour hand is slow: 30 degrees for an hour, 15 for half an hour.

board.text: 12:20. Sana says 120°. How far from the true angle?

At 20 minutes past, the minute hand is exactly on the 4. From the 12 to the 4 is 4 gaps, and 4 times 30 is 120. So far, Sana is right.

choices: No, it has crept towards the 1
ask.ifNot: The hour hand moves all the time. In the 20 minutes since 12 o'clock, it has moved a little way towards the 1.

beats.say: Now the hour hand. Is it exactly on the 12 at 12:20?

ask.ifNot: The hour hand has moved towards the minute hand. The two hands are closer together, so the angle is smaller.

The question asks how far Sana's answer is from the true one. 120 take away 110 is 10.
110 sits in the choices as a trap. It is the true angle, but the question asks for the difference. Sana forgot that the hour hand never waits.

ask.ifNot: Two of the turns are clockwise: the 90 and the 135. Add them. 90 and 135 make 225.

ask.ifNot: Rewinding goes backwards through time. The last thing he did was the 90 anticlockwise turn, so that one is undone first.

To undo a turn, turn the same amount the opposite way. So to undo 90 anticlockwise, we turn 90 clockwise, starting from south.
90 clockwise from south is a quarter turn, and it takes us to west. So between his two turns, Ravi was facing west.

beats.say: Stand where the two angles meet. You face along the line, then turn to face the other way. That is a half turn. So how much do the two angles make together?
A half turn is 180 degrees. So x, plus 27, equals 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So x is 180 take away 27.

beats.say: 180 is the whole, and 27 is one part of it. x is the other part. How do we find x?
Let's take 27 away in two easy hops. First the 20: 180 take away 20 leaves 160.
Now the 7 that is left: 160 take away 7 leaves 153. So 180 minus 27 is 153.
So x equals 153. The other angle is 153 degrees.
Check: 153 plus 27 makes 180, one whole straight line. It fits.
So angles on a straight line always make 180 degrees. Take the one you know away from 180, and you have the other.

board.text: Facing South, then North-East. How did he turn?

beats.say: A man faces south. Later he faces north-east. We have to say how he turned: how many degrees, and which way round.
The 8 compass directions share a full turn of 360 degrees. So each step from one direction to the next is 360 divided by 8, which is 45 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Anticlockwise from south we pass south-east, then east, and then we reach north-east. That is 3 steps.

beats.say: Let's go anticlockwise from south first. That is the opposite way to clock hands. How many steps is it to north-east?
South-east, east, north-east. 3 steps of 45 make 135 degrees, anticlockwise.
Now the other way, clockwise. South-west, west, north-west, north, north-east. That is 5 steps, and 5 times 45 is 225 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The size matches, but the direction does not. 135 clockwise from south passes south-west and west, and stops at north-west. The way round matters.

beats.say: So there are two true ways to say it: 135 anticlockwise, or 225 clockwise. Now the trap. One choice says 135 clockwise. Is that true?

board.text: 135° clockwise from S ends at NW

beats.say: The right size, but the other way round, so it lands on north-west. And none of the choices says 225 clockwise.
So the true statement is: he turned 135 degrees in the anticlockwise direction.
With turning questions, always check two things: how far, and which way round.
We need the supplementary angle to 57 and a quarter degrees.

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do two supplementary angles add up to?
So we take 57 and a quarter away from 180. A mixed number is easier in two bites: first the whole number, then the quarter.
First the 57. 180 take away 50 is 130, and 7 more away leaves 123.

ask.ifNot: We are taking away, so the answer drops just below 123. Break one whole into 4 quarters and take 1 quarter off. That leaves 122 and three quarters.

beats.say: The quarter still has to come off. What is a quarter less than 123?
Take one whole from 123, leaving 122, and cut that whole into 4 quarters. Take 1 quarter away, and three quarters are left.
So the supplementary angle is 122 and three quarters degrees.
Check by adding. 57 and 122 make 179. A quarter and three quarters make 1 more. 180 exactly.
The slip to watch for is adding the quarter back on, instead of taking it off. Whole number first, then the fraction, and both are taken away.

board.text: In 300 seconds the minute hand moves ___ degrees

beats.say: In 300 seconds, how many degrees does the minute hand of a clock move?

ask.ifNot: There are 60 seconds in a minute. 60 times 5 is 300, so 300 seconds is 5 minutes.

beats.say: The minute hand works in minutes, not seconds. So first, how many minutes is 300 seconds?
300 divided by 60 is 5. So we are really asking: how far does the minute hand move in 5 minutes?
In 60 minutes the minute hand goes right round the clock once. That is a full turn, 360 degrees.
So in 1 minute it turns 360 divided by 60. That is 6 degrees each minute.

ask.ifNot: Each minute is 6 degrees, and there are 5 minutes, so it is 5 times 6. 30 degrees is the size of a whole gap between two numbers, not of 1 minute.

beats.say: 5 minutes, at 6 degrees each minute. Which sum tells us how far?
5 times 6 is 30. The minute hand moves 30 degrees.
And that makes sense. In 5 minutes the minute hand goes from one number to the next, like from 12 to 1. That gap is 360 divided by 12, which is 30 as well.
So change the seconds to minutes first. Then it is 6 degrees for every minute.

board.text: Which pair of angles is complementary?

beats.say: Here are 4 pairs of angles. Only one pair is complementary, and we have to find it.

ask.ifNot: Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. A square corner is a right angle, and that is 90 degrees.

beats.say: What must two complementary angles add up to?
So we add each pair and look for 90. 30 and 30 make 60. Too small. 40 and 30 make 70. Still too small.

ask.ifNot: 80 from the tens, and 10 more from the ones. 80 and 10 make 90.

beats.say: Next pair: 22 and 68. Add the ones first: 2 and 8 make 10. Then the tens: 20 and 60 make 80. What is the total?
22 plus 68 is exactly 90. That is our pair.
Let's make sure of the last one too. 34 and 66: 4 and 6 make 10, and 30 and 60 make 90, so that is 100. Too big.
So the complementary pair is 22 degrees and 68 degrees.
Complementary means the two angles fill a square corner exactly. So add the pair, and look for 90 on the dot.
The angle measures 35 degrees. We have two jobs: find its complementary angle and its supplementary angle. Then we add them.

ask.ifNot: A square corner is a right angle, a quarter turn. That is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: First the complement. Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. How much do they make together?
So the complement is 90 take away 35. 90 take away 30 is 60, and 5 more away leaves 55.

ask.ifNot: The two angles on the line make 180 together. So take 35 away from 180.

beats.say: Now the supplement. Supplementary angles sit together on a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees. Which sum gives the supplement?
180 take away 35. Here is a quick way: 180 is 90 more than 90, so the supplement is 90 more than the complement. 55 and 90 make 145.
Careful now. The question wants the sum of the two partners. Not the angle itself. Just the complement and the supplement.
55 plus 145. The tens first: 50 and 140 make 190. Then the ones: 5 and 5 make 10. Altogether, 200.
So the sum is 200 degrees.
C for complementary, C for corner: 90. S for supplementary, S for straight line: 180. Find both partners, then add them.

board.text: Which pair of angles is complementary?

beats.say: 4 pairs of angles, and only one pair is complementary. Let's test them one at a time.

ask.ifNot: A square corner is a right angle, and a right angle is 90 degrees. So the pair must add up to 90.

beats.say: Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. So what must the pair add up to?
First pair: 55 and 45. The two 5s make 10, and 50 and 40 make 90. So that is 100. Too big.

ask.ifNot: 80 from the tens, and 10 more from the two 5s. 80 and 10 make 90.

beats.say: Second pair: 65 and 25. The two 5s make 10 again, and 60 and 20 make 80. So what is the total?
65 plus 25 is exactly 90. That is the pair we want.
A careful mathematician checks the rest. 35 and 48 make 83. 17 and 63 make 80. Neither is 90.
So the complementary pair is 65 degrees and 25 degrees.
The first pair was the tempting one, because 55 and 45 look so neat. But they make 100. Always do the adding.

board.text: Angle between the hands = 45°. What time is it?

beats.say: The teacher's watch shows an angle of 45 degrees between its hands. We have 4 times to choose from, so let's test them.
On a clock, the full turn of 360 degrees is shared by 12 numbers. So each gap between two numbers is 30 degrees.
45 degrees is one whole gap of 30, and half a gap, 15, more. So we want hands that are 1 and a half gaps apart.

ask.ifNot: In half an hour, the hour hand goes half of the way to the next number. So at half past 7 it sits halfway between the 7 and the 8.

beats.say: Three of the times are half past something. At half past, the minute hand is on the 6. But where is the hour hand at half past 7?
That is the trap: the hour hand does not wait on the 7. Now count from the 6. From 6 to 7 is one gap. Then half a gap more. 1 and a half gaps!
And 1 and a half gaps is 45 degrees. So half past 7 fits.
Now the others. At half past 8 the hour hand is one gap further on: 2 and a half gaps, 75 degrees. At half past 2 it is 3 and a half gaps from the 6. Both are too wide.
And at quarter past 1, the minute hand is on the 3 and the hour hand is a little past the 1. That is nearly 2 gaps, which is more than 45 degrees.
So the time is 7:30.
With clock angles, count gaps of 30 degrees. And always ask: where has the hour hand crept to?
Here is 153 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplement is the other piece of that line, the one with the question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 153, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 153.

Let's take 153 away in two easy hops. First the 150: 180 take away 150 leaves 30.
Now the 3 that is left: 30 take away 3 leaves 27. So 180 minus 153 is 27.
So the supplement is 27 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 153 plus 27 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 90 take away 51.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

board.text: More than 90° but less than 180°: called?

beats.say: Here is an angle that is more than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees. What is it called?
Angle names go by size. The small ones, less than 90, are acute. Exactly 90, the square corner, is a right angle.
Now jump to the far end. An angle that opens past a straight line, more than 180, is called reflex.

ask.ifNot: Acute is for angles under 90, and reflex is for angles over 180. The name for the ones in between is obtuse.

beats.say: Our angle is wider than the square corner, but it has not opened out flat. Which name is left for it?
Obtuse. An angle between 90 and 180 degrees is an obtuse angle.
Obtuse means blunt. An acute angle is sharp, like a pencil tip. An obtuse angle is blunt and wide, like a book lying nearly flat.
So, in order of size: acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex. Obtuse sits between the square corner and the straight line.
What kind of angle is 250 degrees? Here it is. It is a big one.
To name an angle, we compare it with the fence posts. 90 is a right angle, 180 is a straight line, and 360 is a full turn.

ask.ifNot: Look at the hundreds. 180 has 1 hundred and 250 has 2 hundreds. So 250 is the bigger number.

beats.say: Is 250 more than 180, or less?
More than 180. So the angle has opened past a straight line. It cannot be obtuse, because obtuse stops at 180.
But 250 is less than 360, so it is not a full turn either. It is not a complete angle.

ask.ifNot: A straight angle is exactly 180, and a complete angle is exactly 360. Anything in between those two is a reflex angle.

beats.say: Past a straight line, but short of a full turn. What do we call an angle like that?
So 250 degrees is a reflex angle.
A reflex angle is the long way round. Whenever the size is between 180 and 360, the angle is reflex.

board.text: Which instrument is used to measure an angle?

beats.say: Open your geometry box. Which of these tools is used to measure an angle?

ask.ifNot: Centimetres are for lengths and grams are for weights. The size of an angle, how far it opens, is measured in degrees.

beats.say: First, what are angles measured in?
Degrees. So we need a tool that has degrees marked on it. Let's check each tool's job.
A compass holds a pencil and draws circles. A pair of dividers has two sharp points, for comparing lengths. No degrees on either.

board.text: Set square: a few fixed angles

beats.say: A set square has a few fixed corners, so it helps to draw some angles. But it cannot measure any angle you like.

ask.ifNot: The half circle with the degree marks is the protractor. A ruler measures length, and a compass draws circles.

beats.say: One tool is left. It is a half circle, with degrees marked all round its curved edge, from 0 to 180. What is it called?
The protractor. That is the tool that measures an angle.
Each tool has its own job. A ruler for lengths, a compass for circles, and a protractor for angles.
We want the complementary angle of 67 and a half degrees.

ask.ifNot: Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. A square corner is a right angle, and that is 90 degrees.

beats.say: What do two complementary angles add up to?
So we take 67 and a half away from 90. Let's do it in two bites: the whole 67 first, then the half.
90 take away 67. 90 take away 60 is 30, and 7 more away leaves 23.

ask.ifNot: We are taking away, so the answer goes just below 23. Half way back from 23 towards 22 is 22 and a half.

beats.say: The half still has to come off. What is half less than 23?
Half less than 23 is 22 and a half.
So the complementary angle is 22 and a half degrees.
Check. 67 and 22 make 89. The two halves make 1 more. 90 exactly.
Whole number first, then the half. Both are taken away, so the answer ends up just below 23, not above it.
We want the supplementary angle of 55 degrees. Here is 55 degrees on a straight line, with its partner beside it.

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do two supplementary angles add up to?
So 55 and its partner make 180. The partner is 180 take away 55.

ask.ifNot: 130 take away 5 is 125. It must end up below 130, because we are taking away.

beats.say: Take the 50 away first. 180 take away 50 is 130. Then the 5. What is 130 take away 5?
125. So 180 take away 55 is 125.
The supplementary angle is 125 degrees.
Check: 55 and 125. The two 5s make 10, and 50 and 120 make 170. 170 and 10 is 180.
The tempting slip is 35. That is 90 take away 55, the complementary angle. S for supplementary, S for straight line: 180.
Here is 10 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplement is the other piece of that line, the one with the question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 10, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 10.

180 take away 10 leaves 170.
So the supplement is 170 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 10 plus 170 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.
This question has two parts. First we find x. Then we find the supplement of x.

ask.ifNot: 90 is the whole and 35 is one part. To find the other part, take 35 away from 90.

beats.say: x and 35 make 90. So x is the missing piece of a square corner. Which sum finds it?
90 take away 30 is 60, and 5 more away is 55. So x is 55 degrees.
Careful. 55 is x, but the question does not stop there. It asks for the supplement of x.

ask.ifNot: We want the supplement of x, and x is 55. So we take 55 away from 180. 180 take away 35 would be the supplement of the other angle.

beats.say: A supplement is the partner that makes a straight line, 180 degrees. So which sum do we need now?
180 take away 50 is 130, and 5 more away is 125.
So the supplement of x is 125 degrees.
Check: 55 and 125 make 180. And in a two part question, read the last line again before you choose.

board.text: Supplement of an angle = 125°. Its complement = ?

beats.say: We are not told the angle. We are told its supplement, 125 degrees. And we are asked for its complement.

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So first we must find the angle itself. An angle and its supplement make how much together?
So the angle is 180 take away 125. Count up from 125: 5 more gets to 130, and 50 more gets to 180. That is 55.

ask.ifNot: The complement belongs to the angle itself, which is 55. Complementary angles make 90, so take 55 away from 90.

beats.say: Now for what the question asks: the complement of this angle. A complement is the partner that makes a square corner. Which sum is it?
90 take away 55 is 35.
So the complement is 35 degrees.
Check both. 55 and 125 make 180: that is the supplement. 55 and 35 make 90: that is the complement.
One choice says the angle has no complement. That only happens when an angle is 90 or more. Ours is 55, so it has one. Find the angle first, then its partner.

board.text: Two lines cross. Pairs of opposite angles = ?

beats.say: Two lines cross, like the letter X. How many pairs of vertically opposite angles do they make?
Two crossing lines make 4 angles round the crossing point. I have called them a, b, c and d.

ask.ifNot: b and d are next door to a, one on each side. The one straight across the crossing point is c.

beats.say: Vertically opposite angles face each other across the crossing point. Which angle is straight across from a?
a faces c. That is one pair.
Two angles are left, b and d. They face each other too. That is a second pair.
Every angle is in a pair now. So there are 2 pairs of vertically opposite angles.
The slip to avoid is saying 4. That is the number of angles. They match up across the point, 2 by 2, so there are 2 pairs.

board.text: Lines intersect: one angle is 70°. Opposite = ?

beats.say: Two lines cross, and one of the angles is 70 degrees. We want the angle opposite to it, straight across the crossing point.

ask.ifNot: Two angles side by side on a straight line make a half turn together. A half turn is 180 degrees.

beats.say: Look at the angle next door, called p. It shares a straight line with the 70. What do two angles on a straight line make together?
So p is 180 take away 70, which is 110.

ask.ifNot: 180 take away 110 leaves 70. You can check: 110 and 70 make 180.

beats.say: Now p and our mystery angle share the other straight line. So the mystery angle is 180 take away 110. What is that?
70. The very same as the angle we started with!
That always happens. Angles straight across a crossing are called vertically opposite, and they are always equal.
So next time there is nothing to work out: the opposite angle is equal. 110 is the neighbour on the line, not the angle across.
Here is 85 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplement is the other piece of that line, the one with the question mark.

board.text: Linear pair: one angle is 65°. The other = ?

beats.say: Two angles form a linear pair, and one of them is 65 degrees. We want the other one.

ask.ifNot: Two angles side by side on a straight line make a half turn together. A half turn is 180 degrees.

beats.say: The word linear has line inside it. A linear pair is two angles side by side on a straight line. So what do they add up to?
So 65, plus the other angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: 5 less than 120 is 115. We are taking away, so we land below 120.

beats.say: We need 180 take away 65. First take away 60, which leaves 120. Then take 5 more. What is left?
115. So 180 take away 65 is 115.
The other angle is 115 degrees.
Check: 65 and 115. 60 and 110 make 170, and the two 5s make 10 more. 180.
The two angles of a linear pair do not have to be equal. They just have to make a straight line together: 180 degrees.

board.text: Angle between the hands at 3 o'clock = ?

beats.say: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand at 3 o'clock? Here is the clock.

ask.ifNot: Share 360 among the 12 gaps. 12 times 30 is 360, so each gap is 30 degrees.

beats.say: The 12 numbers cut the clock face into 12 equal gaps, and all the way round is a full turn of 360 degrees. So how big is one gap?
360 divided by 12 is 30. Each gap is 30 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps: 12 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3. That is 3 gaps.

beats.say: At 3 o'clock the minute hand points straight up at the 12, and the hour hand points at the 3. How many gaps are between them?
3 gaps of 30 make 90 degrees.
So the angle is 90 degrees.
And look at the clock. The hands make a perfect square corner, and 90 degrees is a right angle. Count the gaps, then times by 30.
What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand at 9:30? This one has a catch.
Each gap between two numbers on a clock is 30 degrees, because 360 shared among 12 gaps is 30.

Halfway between the 9 and the 10. So we count in two parts. First, from the 6 to the 9. That is 3 gaps, and 3 times 30 is 90.
Then the extra half gap, past the 9. Half of 30 is 15.

We want the supplement of 165 degrees. Supplementary angles are two angles that sit side by side on a straight line. Here is the picture.

board.text: At which time is the angle between the hands obtuse?

beats.say: At which of these 4 times do the clock hands make an obtuse angle? We need to test each time.

ask.ifNot: Obtuse means wider than a right angle, 90 degrees, but not yet a straight line, 180 degrees.

beats.say: First, what makes an angle obtuse?
On a clock, each gap between two numbers is 30 degrees. So 90 degrees is 3 gaps, and 180 degrees is 6 gaps. We want more than 3 gaps, but fewer than 6.
Start with the o'clock times. At 10 o'clock the minute hand points straight up, and the hour hand is on the 10, only 2 gaps away. 60 degrees. That is acute.
At 6 o'clock the hands are 6 gaps apart, pointing opposite ways. Exactly 180. That is a straight angle, and an obtuse angle must be less than 180.

ask.ifNot: By half past, the hour hand has gone half of the way to the next number. So it is halfway between the 3 and the 4.

beats.say: Now half past 3. The minute hand is on the 6. Careful: where is the hour hand?
So from the hour hand to the 6 is 2 and a half gaps. 60, and 15 more, is 75 degrees. Acute again. Leaving the hand on the 3 would give 90, and that is the trap.
That leaves 4 o'clock. The hands are 4 gaps apart, and 4 times 30 is 120. More than 90, and less than 180.
So the angle is obtuse at 4 o'clock.
For each time: find both hands, count the gaps, and times by 30. Then name the angle.

board.text: When do the hands form a straight angle (180°)?

beats.say: When do the two hands of a clock form a straight angle, 180 degrees? We have three times to test.

ask.ifNot: 6 times 30 is 180. So the hands must be exactly 6 gaps apart, half way round the clock from each other.

beats.say: A straight angle means the hands point in exactly opposite directions. Each gap between two numbers on a clock is 30 degrees. So 180 degrees is how many gaps?
6 gaps of 30 make 180. So we want the hands exactly 6 gaps apart.
At 6 o'clock the minute hand points straight up, and the hour hand is exactly on the 6, straight down. 6 gaps apart. A perfect straight line.

choices: No, it has moved towards the 4
ask.ifNot: The hour hand never stops. After 45 minutes it has gone three quarters of the way from the 3 to the 4.

beats.say: Now 3:45. The minute hand is on the 9, and the 9 is opposite the 3. But is the hour hand still on the 3?
It has crept most of the way to the 4. So the hands are not exactly opposite any more.
It is the same story at 9:15. The minute hand is on the 3, opposite the 9. But the hour hand has moved a little past the 9. Close to a straight line, but not exact.
So the hands form a straight angle only at 6 o'clock.
All of these was the trap. It only looks true if the hour hand waits on its number. It never does, except exactly on the hour.

board.text: At which time is the angle between the hands greatest?

Every gap between two numbers on a clock is the same size, 30 degrees. So to begin with we can just count gaps. The most gaps wins.
9 o'clock is the easy one. The hour hand is exactly on the 9 and the minute hand is on the 12. That is 3 gaps.

ask.ifNot: From halfway past the 4, it is half a gap to reach the 5, and then one more gap to the 6. That is 1 and a half gaps.

1 and a half gaps. That is small. Not our winner.
Now the two quarter past times. In 15 minutes, a quarter of an hour, the hour hand creeps a quarter of a gap forward. That little creep decides everything.
At 12:15 the minute hand is on the 3. The hour hand has crept a little past the 12, towards the 3. So the angle shrinks: a bit less than 3 gaps.

ask.ifNot: From the 3 to the 6 is 3 gaps. The hour hand has moved on past the 6, further from the 3. So the angle has grown a little.

beats.say: At 6:15 the minute hand is on the 3 again. But the hour hand has crept past the 6, away from the 3. Is the angle bigger or smaller than 3 gaps?
A bit more than 3 gaps. That beats 9 o'clock, which is exactly 3.
So the greatest angle is at 6:15.
3 gaps are exactly 90 degrees. So 6:15 is just past a right angle, and 12:15 is just short of one.
The hour hand's small creep matters. Always ask which way it creeps: towards the other hand, or away from it.

board.text: At 1 o'clock the angle is 30°. Complementary angle at?

So the angle we want is 90 take away 30. That is 60 degrees.
